newsitem.title: USA: No evidence of missile in TWA crash - NTSB chief.
newsitem.headline: No evidence of missile in TWA crash - NTSB chief.

text.p: National Transportation Safety Board Chairman James Hall said on Monday there was no physical evidence that a bomb or missile brought down TWA Flight 800, and he was certain investigators would find the cause.
"I'm confident we will find what caused this accident," he told a meeting of the National Air Transportation Association.

Hall said the TWA investigation had cost $27 million but declined to speculate on when investigators might determine the cause and would not comment on published reports that the FBI had attempted to reconstruct the way in which an attacker might have launched a missile at the plane.

The Paris-bound Boeing 747 exploded and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off Long Island on July 17, just minutes after taking off from New York's Kennedy International Airport. All 230 passengers and crew on board were killed.
Hall said the NTSB had reconstructed more than 90 percent of the TWA jetliner and continued to do explosives and other testing.
NTSB investigators were studying a tape of "a Russian stinger missile hitting a civilian plane in Afghanistan" turned over by the NTSB's Russian counterpart several months ago, Hall said.

Investigators had also listened to a flight recorder tape of a fuel-related explosion on a Boeing 737 in the Philippines. That sound seemed closest to the sound of the explosion on board the TWA jet, Hall said.
"We have no physical evidence of a bomb or missile," he said. "We are not going to rule out any of these three items" -- a fuel-related explosion, bomb or missile.
Speaking on both the TWA crash and the May 1996 ValuJet crash in Florida's Everglades, Hall said his agency would have additional safety recommendations for aviation regulators.

The 30-year-old NTSB, with a staff of 350, has no regulatory or enforcement powers, but Hall estimated that about 80 percent of the agency's recommendations were put into effect by legislation or regulation. He expressed frustration with the slow speed at which recommendations were implemented.

In the ValuJet crash, the suspected cause was a fire that may have been started or fueled by mishandled oxygen generators in the plane's cargo hold. The NTSB had recommended years ago that fire detection and suppression equipment be required in the cargo holds of passenger aircraft.
"We recommended that in 1988," he said. "We reiterated it after the ValuJet crash."
